maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister explain what steps have been taken by the government to assist Canadian citizens who may have been caught on the continent of Europe or who are at present in China or Japan or countries in the orient where there may be trouble?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In respect to citizens of Canada who are on the continent of Europe, we have in London at the present time, in addition to the high commissioner and officials of the high commissioner's office, our diplomatic representation which was formerly sent to France and to Holland and to Belgium. The charge d'affaires of the former legations has taken such steps as he has found possible to get particulars of Canadian citizens who are in different parts of Europe, and to make representations in such ways as are possible to secure their exit to Canada or to London from the country in which they may be at the present time. We are endeavouring also to supply them with such financial assistance .as they may require where that is essential toward securing their maintenance and exit.
The situation differs in different countries. As my hon. friend knows, of Canadian citizens who were in France, some are in the occupied
area and some in the unoccupied area. No Canadian nationals have been interned in nonoccupied France and arrangements are being made to provide facilities for the repatriation to Canada of individuals who desire to leave non-occupied France. Some difficulty has been encountered in securing exit permits. The chief difficulties are in securing transportation and permission to cross Spain. The number affected is, however, very small. The United States authorities in France, occupied and nonoccupied, have been authorized to pay up to a maximum of $45 United States funds a month to Canadian nationals, depending upon their needs. No one may secure more, no matter how much his holdings in Canada may be. Recipients are required to sign receipts and pay the moneys advanced out of their accounts in Canada. In case of necessity the necessary funds are advanced if the recipient or his or her family is not financially able to provide for reimbursement. Approximately 60 individuals or families are affected.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the government any knowledge of any Canadian nationals being interned in occupied France?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canadian
nationals, as well as other British subjects of military age who remained in German occupied France after the French collapse were interned by the German authorities. Approximately ninety men who are Canadian nationals have been interned near Paris. The next of kin have been informed so far as possible. By decree of December 5 the German authorities extended the internment order to include women and children who are British subjects, alleging that this action was taken in retaliation for the action of the British authorities in interning German women and children in England. The total number of British subjects so interned is approximately 3,000. They are interned at Caserne Yauban, not far from the Swiss border. We have not been able to ascertain how many Canadian women and children are included. The United States authorities who are looking after Canadian interests in France state that it is expected that the names of any Canadian women and children who have been interned will be notified to them, as the protecting power.
So far as Asia is concerned, some months ago the government notified Canadian nationals in Japan that it would be the part of wisdom for them to secure passage home. We were not at all certain that their leaving the country was imperative, but conditions were such as caused the government to feel it was advisable to make sure that as many as possible did leave Japan at as early a time
Supply-External Affairs

as possible, having regard to the time at which the notice was given to them. I have particulars with regard to the situation there.
Owing to the increased tension in the far east, continuous attention has been given to the problem affecting Canadian nationals in the event of the development of a serious crisis. As early as October, 1940, the Canadian legation in Tokyo was instructed to advise women, and children and others whose presence was not absolutely essential to leave as soon as possible. A further warning was issued on October 25. At that time it was suggested that all Canadians should consider the advisability of arranging for their early repatriation. A third warning was issued on February 6, 1941. Of the 543 Canadians known to be in the far east in August, 1940, exclusive of the legation staff at Tokyo and Japanese Canadians, a certain number have moved to safer areas. Approximately 200 have returned to Canada, and it is estimated that some 177 have remained in what might be considered the danger zone. I understand that most of the number that are remaining belong to religious orders. They have felt that they ought to stay at their posts regardless of what the situation might be.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As yet no minister to Japan has been appointed, although the post has been vacant for some years. It does seem peculiar that an appointment has not been made. Will the Prime Minister explain to the committee the reason for this and will he state whether it is expected that an appointment will be made shortly?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are fortunate in having as charge d'affaires at Tokyo an exceptionally able member of the diplomatic service, Mr. McGreer. He has had experience in the legations at Paris and Washington, and in the department at Ottawa. He is one of the career men and is well qualified to fill the post of charge d'affaires. He served under the former minister at Tokyo. From time to time the government has had different persons under consideration for this particular post.
I may say that, since the war, there has been a great demand for persons who are prepared to give outstanding service in the different branches of the public service. Some of those who have been considered for the position of minister to Japan have taken on other work which they considered more urgent.
I might cite a particular case. I had in view the appointment of General Odium as minister from Canada to Tokyo. General Odium has taken an interest in oriental questions and is particularly well informed on the situation in British Columbia. I thought I had succeeded in having him accept that 
appointment. As, however, the committee knows, General Odium has been appointed to command the second division overseas.
Other names have been considered, but special circumstances have made it difficult to secure the person who the government felt was most desirable for this position in Japan. We would wish to have someone with special qualifications. Just at this particular time it has not been possible to secure the person we would wish to have, all circumstances considered. If there had been any reason to assume that Canada's interests and the interests of our nationals who are in Japan were not being carefully looked after by the legation staff at the present time, some further appointment certainly would have been made. But we have every reason to feel that the interests of Canadian nationals and the interests of the government in relation to Japan are being carefully cared for at the present time.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be a matter of public interest, I think, if, following up the discussion in respect of Canadian nationals, the Prime Minister would be good enough to tell us if he knows the number of Canadian nationals in Germany, Norway and in the low countries, so that we may get a true picture of just what the situation is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend that information.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose they are in with the British.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I could not hear the Prime Minister's reply. Am I right in understanding that there are international regulations governing the treatment accorded to prisoners of war, and are there similar regulations governing the treatment to be accorded to Canadians who might be in Germany or in German-occupied countries? If so, has the Prime Minister any information as to the treatment that has been accorded to Canadians who are still in German-occupied territory?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right in assuming that the treatment accorded to prisoners of war is subject to international convention. We in Canada are taking care to see that Germans who are interned here are treated properly, and we hope that Canadians who are interned in the countries of Europe are being similarly treated. If we had reason to believe that they were not being treated in accordance with international usage, every effort would be put forth to see that proper representations were made and the situation corrected so far as that was possible.

Supply-External Affairs

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is provision in the convention, as I recall it, for a periodical inspection to be made of the internment camps in Britain, we will say, or Canada, by a representative of the other belligerents, and we have the same right to make a periodical inspection of our nationals who are internees or prisoners of war in Germany or German-occupied territory. Has Canada taken any steps to see that the terms of the convention are being carried out by Germany, or is that left to the British government or the government of the United States?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The work of supervision in that respect is carried out for Canada by United States representatives, and we get reports from them.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a complete answer.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask if appointments have been made of ambassadors to Brazil and the Argentine, and, if not, when they will be made?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This committee will be asked to consider an item of expenditure to make provision for legations in the Argentine and Brazil, but until financial provision has been made it would not be possible to make an appointment. I assume that there is little doubt that the house will approve the recommendation of the government to make provision for the appointment of ministers to the Argentine and to Brazil, but the appointments must await the appropriations by parliament.
Speaking of the representation of Canada in South America, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) this afternoon expressed a point of view which, it seems to me, will naturally present itself to many who are considering the question of the wider representation of Canada in other parts of the world. My hon. friend felt that this was perhaps not the best time to incur that increased expenditure. On the other hand, the hon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Gold-well) expressed the contrary view and said that he felt that at this particular time it was very desirable that Canada should have representation in the south American countries. The two points of view afford opportunity for debate, and I can assure hon. members that both have been taken into consideration very carefully by the government.
One of the reasons why the government feel that it is desirable to open legations in Brazil and the Argentine is that for some time past each of those countries has been desirous of opening legations in Ottawa. They have felt that it was in the interests of their countries to come into closer contact with Canada.
Their association with north America up to the present, so far as diplomatic representation is concerned, has been confined to the United States and Mexico, and they feel it would be to their advantage to be represented here.
Our government has precisely the same feeling about the representation of Canada in the two largest republics in south America, that this is a time when great changes are taking place in the world, that south America is likely from now on to have a much closer relationship in business affairs and in matters affecting government and the like with the continent of north America than she has ever had in the past. Unquestionably south American problems will become increasingly our problems as the situation in Europe comes to be changed for better or for worse in the course of the years now beginning, and the government feel that we owe it to the people of our country to be able to get first-hand knowledge of the changing situation in south America and that we should not leave that field, so far as relationships between countries are concerned, exclusively to other countries, leaving Canada the one country in this hemisphere with no diplomatic representation in south America.
There is the further point which I mentioned the other day, that all matters of trade are becoming increasingly matters with which governments must of necessity have some concern. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition said that he would like to see commercial agents keep more in touch with business men. When it comes to the import and export of commodities, licences have to be obtained and all kinds of controls are exercised. Unless the exporting country has some diplomatic agent in the other country who can make representations on its behalf, it is very likely to be completely ignored in international transactions of the kind. We have been fortunate in having wherever we felt we should make use of it the British diplomatic service, but just as we have found it to be to the advantage of Canada to have our own representation at Washington, Paris and elsewhere, so we believe we shall find it of equal advantage to have our own representation in south American countries.
Speaking on this matter, I should say that other Latin-American republics have pressed for an exchange of ministers with Canada. We have hitherto felt, and I think rightly, that we should begin our representation in south America in the two largest republics, and later on consider its extension to other countries of south America. I should speak perhaps of Chile in particular, but we have felt that until the two legations are opened
Supply-External Affairs

and we see what progress is made as a result, we should not for the present ask parliament to extend our representation.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the Department of External Affairs have to consider educating our representatives in south American countries in the Spanish language, or will that be undertaken by our universities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no doubt that we shall have to consider very carefully whatever appointments are made. We shall take care to see that whatever is required in the way of necessary Spanish assistance will be obtained in a manner that will be satisfactory to Canada.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In view of the occupation of France and the low countries, would the minister say just where our representatives-Jean Desy, for instance-are at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my hon. friend is aware, when Holland and Belgium were overrun, the minister and staffs at both Brussels and. the Hague were obliged to leave, and indeed, only got away-

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: By the skin of their teeth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; as my hon. friend says, pretty much by the skin of their teeth. Certainly they had a very rapid exit, and one filled with considerable adventure. The legation staffs, however, moved to London. Mr. Desy was the minister at the Hague and at Brussels. For some months he was in London. He has since come back to Canada, and was in Montreal for a short time making a very complete report to the government on some matters of which he thought we should be informed. At the present time he is in the Department of External Affairs in Ottawa, on special duty.
As my hon. friend is aware, Colonel Georges Vanier is the minister to France. The government felt that Colonel Vanier would be not only a most acceptable but a most desirable member of the permanent joint defence board between Canada and the United States, and we asked him to come to Canada and for the time being to accept appointment on that board. That is the position which Colonel Vanier is filling at the present time.
Mr. Dupuy was made charge d'affaires when Colonel Vanier left. Mr. Dupuy has his headquarters in London. He has been to France, keeping in touch with the government there. Other members-

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not asking the Prime Minister to go into detail.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the present time Mr. Dupuy is acting as charge d'affaires of Canadian representation to the Netherlands and Belgian governments.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose that the decrease in these estimates is accounted for by the fact that the legations themselves are not functioning as such.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has had to be a considerable readjustment. In some instances as much in the way of representation is not required.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder whether the Prime Minister would mind making a statement respecting what progress, if any, has been made on the St. Lawrence treaty? This matter is of great interest to my constituency. In common with other representatives I have been endeavouring to get some information over a period of many weeks. As a matter of fact, within the last two months I was with a delegation before the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) here, when it was suggested to us that possibly we should go to Toronto for our information; I think the minister's words were that it was "a baby of the Ontario government". From what I see in the press I have come to the conclusion that possibly it is a baby of the United States government.
I am particularly interested because apparently the scheme which is now being discussed is one which has never been under consideration before. It is impossible to get any definite information or to obtain maps showing the water levels. This means a great deal to my constituency; I believe that some 26,000 acres of the earliest settled land in Ontario will be covered by water if a single stage scheme is carried out. I understand that such plans are in existence, and, at the time the delegation were before the Minister of Public Works, we received a promise from him that at some time those plans would be available, so that the people in that district would see what they were likely to suffer as the result of a development under a single stage plan. Although my information is indefinite, I have been told that these plans are in existence. When the Prime Minister is making a statement on this point, would he say where such plans can be seen?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know that I can say more at the moment with respect to the St. Lawrence waterway project than to mention that, as I think my hon. friend is already aware, the subject is a matter of negotiation at the present time between the United States government and the Canadian government. Until those negotiations are

Supply-External Affairs
completed, when and if they are, I am hardly in a position to indicate to the committee what the nature of the agreement is to be. When my hon. friend says it differs from anything which has been considered before, he probably refers to only one phase of the agreement. The committee will recall that an agreement in the nature of a treaty was made between the government of Mr. Bennett and the government of the United States, but the United States Senate failed to sanction it. Further negotiations have taken a somewhat different form.
The view has been held that all the waterway problems, as far as it is possible to connect them, should be brought together into one agreement and dealt with there; that is to say, matters affecting power, navigation, the levels of the waters on the lakes, scenic aspects at Niagara, and the like. An agreement covering all of these interrelated problems has been under consideration by both governments more or less continuously for some time past. Any agreement which is reached will of necessity involve an agreement between the provincial government and the dominion government as to matters affecting Ontario. There will have to be an agreement or understanding with the province of Quebec with respect to matters affecting that province. I have always taken the position that, with respect to an international agreement, we would desire first to settle matters between our own provinces and the dominion government before we finally reached an agreement with another country. We have not yet completed the negotiations with either the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec. I hope that they will not take long to complete. If they are completed, the next stage would be to continue negotiations with the United States.
My hon. friend's question at the close related, I believe, more particularly to the one stage plan and the two stage plan development at Morrisburg. I cannot say offhand to him at the moment where these particular plans may be seen, but I shall make inquiries and, if they are available for inspection, give him a further answer later on.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we
understand the Prime Minister aright, the whole position is still in the negotiation stage, and therefore he is not in a position to make any statement as to what may be done. And, anterior to arriving at the agreement there must be, as he said, an agreement with the two provinces, because some of their rights, I assume, are to be affected. As I understand the legal position, the only jurisdiction this government has is with regard to navigation. If it were solely a question of power, which
I believe it to be, the major part of the jurisdiction would, of course, rest in the provinces, because I think it is an accepted fact that in law power that may be generated out of the Canadian development belongs to the provinces.
There is another aspect of the matter I might touch upon. When the previous arrangement was negotiated it was in the form of a treaty. Under their constitution that treaty had to go for confirmation and sanction to the senate of the United States. Is it proposed to follow the same practice in this, or is it proposed, as I have seen suggested, that by some stretch of the powers contained in the boundary waters treaty, it may be entered into as a mere agreement which would not require the assent of a two-thirds majority of the senate, as a treaty would in the United States, but merely a majority in both houses of congress?
I have taken the trouble to read the boundary waters treaty of 1909-10, and I venture the opinion that it was never the intention of *the high contracting parties to the treaty that an agreement involving the international section of the St. Lawrence waterway should be entered into as a mere agreement. There is no power there, and I would ask the Prime Minister whether the opinion of the Department of Justice has been taken on that particular phase of the question. If so, will he table it?
My own view is, and it is agreed to by others whose legal opinion I value, that the provisions of the treaty of 1909-10 do not contain powers to make an agreement of this kind respecting the development of a huge project such as would be developed at Morrisburg. It must be followed by a treaty. If the Prime Minister has an opinion on that point, as to the jurisdiction to proceed, not by way of treaty but by mere agreement, I should like to have that legal opinion tabled so that we might study it. The matter is of importance especially so far as the other high contracting party is concerned. As regards Canada, we have not the same constitutional provision. The treaty or agreement or whatever it may be, would, I assume, be submitted to parliament for adoption. If it is a treaty, it has to go to the United States senate to be confirmed by a two-thirds vote of that body. If it is a mere agreement, then it has only to carry the affirmative vote of a majority of both houses of congress. The Prime Minister will be seized of what I am suggesting. Has he taken an opinion on that point and, if so, is it available?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I understand
that the United States government itself has been considering whether in the public inter-
Supply-External Affairs

ests it would be preferable to have the understanding between Canada and the United States with respect to navigation and power on the St. Lawrence made in the form of an agreement between the two countries, which would be approved by a resolution of both houses, alike in the United States and Canada, or whether it should take the form of a treaty. There are arguments pro and con. The argument with respect to agreement is that if work is to be done it is likely to be pressing, and the more rapidly money can be procured for the purposes of development, the more expeditiously the work will be proceeded with. Whether or not the United States intends to press that aspect of the question I cannot say at the moment, but so far as we are concerned the Department of Justice has been looking into the very question which the hon. gentleman has raised, and I shall be in a position when a decision has been reached, to give him an opinion from the department regarding the legal point he has raised.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As soon
as convenient, if the opinion is available, I should like to have it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For
the purpose of keeping the record clear may I point out that both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition have referred to the Morrisburg scheme. As a matter of fact, the Morrisburg scheme is the one referred to as scheme B in the report of the Hydro Electric Power commission engineers of 1921. Scheme B has never been considered from that time. There is no dam at Morrisburg under the scheme which I understand is being considered at the present time. Complete power development under the scheme which is now being considered is at Barnhart island. The new idea in the scheme is to have a control dam at the village of Iroquois, which village incidentally is to be wiped out. The control dam in itself is not a new scheme, because prior to 1921-as a matter of fact as far back as the days of the late Sir Adam Beck -a control dam was considered. Its location was not defined, but at least it was not at the village of Iroquois.
The scheme being considered at the present time develops power estimated at 2,200,000 horse power at Barnhart island. The control dam is at the village of Iroquois, and it is a dam which is not used for the purpose of developing power.
May I say again that my constituency is particularly interested because, under the previous treaty, which it was attempted to negotiate in 1932, only 9,000 acres of land was flooded. Under this scheme 26,000 acres will

be flooded, the greater part of which is on the Canadian side of the river. This is due to the fact that the banks on this side are much lower than on the United States side. I suggested in my first remarks on the subject that this was some of the first occupied land in Ontario. As a matter of fact, the occupancy of the land, the grants of title to the land go back to 1784. Many sites along the front in a distance of a few miles are most historical. The first church, the celebration of the 150th anniversary of which was held in 1934, is in this district. There is a memorial church and there are numerous cemeteries. Although the people in that district are told that their compensation will be such that they will have no worries after the project is completed, I assure hon. members and the people of the district that, afteT the project is completed, if it is completed' on the basis of a single-stage development, there will be more heart-burnings in the district than there have been in the previous one hundred and fifty-five years of its existence.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the Prime Minister make a statement regarding the personnel of the permanent joint board of defence, the authority they have, and what has been accomplished to date?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not the names of the members of the permanent board, but I shall have them to-morrow. As to the powers of the board, they have powers of investigation of matters of joint defence on both Atlantic and Pacific coasts and the making of recommendations to the respective governments. The recommendations come in the form of reports from the board to the government of the United States and the Canadian government. The recommendations considered by the Canadian government are those relating to matters of defence for which, if the work is to be performed, Canada must undertake the responsibility. When the reports are received by the Canadian government, they are referred to the departments of the government to which the work itself relates. For example, if the work relates to naval defence, the report on that subject goes to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. If the work relates to air activities, it goes to the air minister. The matter is considered by the military experts in the department and the war committee of the cabinet on the recommendation of the minister decides whether or not the work is to be carried out.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition spoke about commitments, and said he found difficulty in understanding how there could be no commitments. I hope I have made it clear that while the board has power to make

Supply-External Affairs
recommendations to the government, the government itself decides whether or not those recommendations should be carried out and the work undertaken.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is quite clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But that is not in the nature of any commitment which Canada is under to the United States or which the United States is under to Canada. There is nothing in the nature of an obligation on the part of either government to carry out what the joint committee recommends except in so far as the government itself is prepared to take that step. That was what I meant in saying there were no commitments.
As to what has been done, I think perhaps the committee will agree that there is nothing in the nature of military secrets which should be kept more a secret than practically everything contained in the reports which have been made on the joint defence of Canada and the United States. We could not bring down those reports in this parliament without disclosing matters affecting the defence of the United States as well as our own coast defence. It would not do to publish that information; it is the information above all else that the enemy would wish to have. That is the sole reason for not publishing the reports.
I have here the names of the Canadian members of the permanent joint board. They are: Colonel O. M. Biggar, chairman; Brigadier Stewart, Air-Commodore Cuffe, Captain H. E. Reid, Colonel G. P. Vanier, H. L. Keenleyside, secretary.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister if in this connection he is getting the full cooperation of the province of Ontario. Within the last five hours I had dinner at Brockville, where I saw a corps of engineers of the Ontario hydro electric, with blueprints and what not, who are working on this project. The question I am asking is whether we are getting the full cooperation of the Ontario government with regard to this St. Lawrence development.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot answer that question until an actual agreement between Ontario and the dominion has been reached. I have every reason to believe that for some time past there has been a disposition on the part of the government of Ontario to cooperate with this government in matters pertaining to the St. Lawrence. Whether or not all the questions that have to be considered have thus far been taken up, I am not in a position to say.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just
anxious to get from the Prime Minister a
statement that as far as the general plan is concerned, as it is being developed by the dominion authority, it is in unison with the general plan of the province of Ontario with regard to the development of power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think that is correct.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know whether or not I should ask the Prime Minister, but one question that arose a year or two ago was that of the export of power. I realize that the Prime Minister may not be able to answer that question now, but if he can, would he tell the committee whether or not any agreement with Ontario is predicated on the question of the export of power?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply has been conducting negotiations with the Ontario government, on behalf of the federal government. This evening he told me there were some matters still to be considered. The question my hon. friend has mentioned may be among that number, but I am not in a position to say definitely.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no desire to hold up the Prime Minister's estimates, which are not ordinarily of a contentious nature, but my colleague the hon. member for Broadview would like to speak on this subject to-morrow, so I would ask the Prime Minister to call it eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend not allow one item to go through?

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, yes. Will we take up these estimates to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. I may say to my hon. friend that I am anxious to get through the estimates of the Department of External Affairs in order that I may give attention to other very pressing matters.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We shall be very glad to help the Prime Minister get them through.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps the Prime Minister would be kind enough to say that he will give us some statement with regard to the question of licences for the export of power under this development.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think until we have concluded negotiations with the province of Ontario, any matters that are likely to arise in connection with those negotiations would be better left over. I prefer not to make a statement at the present time.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps it will come after instead of before.
Supply-External Affairs

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I understand there are still a number of members who wish to ask some questions with regard to these estimates. If the request of our leader in regard to the hon. member for Broadview is granted, will it apply also to other members on this side?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose if we had strictly followed the customary practice, we would have confined discussion to the particular item before the committee. I think we have discussed everything but that item. I would not ask that the item be passed except with the understanding that on other items the same general discussion may be carried on, if it is so desired.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the Prime Minister will agree that on the administration item the discussion usually is of the widest character, but that we are confined to the particular items in subsequent discussions. To-morrow we will facilitate the passage of these estimates, but several hon. members do wish to speak, and I would ask the Prime Minister to report progress now.

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With that understanding; or is it absolutely necessary for the Prime Minister's purpose to get an item through to-night? I do not know the technical position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR-PRESENT POSITION  CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION OP THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; it is not
necessary at all.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 25, 1941.
